judge: judge-3, people P21-P30, draft 1 wording as printed in results.json

problems: Benedict is a good surprise for a quiet, conscientious Presbyterian who goes to 5 a.m. dawn prayer (Benedict's monks rose for Vigils). The grace line ('credit it to God, not to himself') is exactly his Strongly disagree on effort.
Benedict's 'tell' line ends on a comma ('...root them out,') and is about the abbot's duty to root out faults. It reads harsher than Kim's mild Agree about telling a friend.

Origen's 'mystery' line starts mid-sentence in lower case ('while on other subjects...'), runs long in archaic English and is cut off with an ellipsis before the point. He cannot tell from it that Origen means the apostles left gaps on purpose for lovers of wisdom to explore.

The Origen line he would feel most is not shown: 'In the end, God will save everyone' (Origen yes, Kim a slow Disagree, thinking of his Buddhist grandmother). It lost the tie to 'mystery' only because of statement order.
Source names vary for the same book: 'Rule of St Benedict', 'Rule of Benedict', 'The Rule'.

Ambrose is right for a woman who feeds any neighbour who is short: 'The earth belongs to all, not to the rich' is the best line in her reveal. His warning against those who say 'Touch me not, for I am pure' fits her Strongly disagree on putting people out. But 'forsooth' and 'delicate ones' make it hard to read.
The quiet line from Ambrose fits her proverb about flies and a closed mouth. It is a lovely match.
The kindred result is a coin flip: Ambrose 0.41, Nazianzen 0.40.

Hilary is a weak sparring partner. He is farthest only at -0.37, on 6 statements, and every clash is small. His lines are about philosophy and the state, the part she said 'sounded like a university'.

Hilary's 'It is the time to speak, because the time for keeping silent is now past' is a battle cry against the emperor Constantius. It is not a view that people should generally talk more, so it does not really disagree with 'better to say less'.
Hilary's learning line is cut off with an ellipsis in the middle of 'Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after...', which is archaic and incomplete.
The dates line for Ambrose is long and formatted unlike the others ('born c. 339-340 at Trier; bishop of Milan from 374; died 4 April 397 at Milan').
people.better: Sparring: John Chrysostom. The data already has him clashing with her hard on three things she lives by: laughter (she laughs loudly; he says play comes from the devil, not God), weeping (she cries easily; he rebuked loud mourning at funerals) and keeping sinners out (she says no; he barred them from communion). Each is a full -4 clash, against Hilary's -2s. He also shares her love of the poor, which makes him a sparring partner she would enjoy arguing with.

problems: Nazianzen is a very good emotional fit for a man burned by church politics who prays on mountain ridges. He was made a bishop against his will, resigned, and asked to go home to 'my desert, my country life, and my God'. The hook does the work, but the lines do not.
Nazianzen's education line is long, archaic and cut off before the point, that pagan learning is good too.

Nazianzen's purity line needs context: 'O new Pharisee... who dischargest upon us the sentiments of Novatus'. Few readers know Novatus, and 'dischargest' is hard to read. The closing 'Will you not give any place to weeping?' is the part that lands.

Benedict's laughter line is perfect for a sarcastic man ('buffoonery... we utterly condemn'), and the silence rule ('do not speak until he is spoken to') is exactly the old-church control he is wary of.

Benedict's third line (learning) is not Benedict's own words. It is Gregory the Great's narration in the Dialogues, it is cut off before 'learned ignorance', and it does not clearly disagree with learning from outsiders.

Jerome is the best kindred in this set. He was a fasting, Scripture-obsessed scholar, impatient with lukewarm Christians, and his hook is the dream before the judgment seat. Imran came to faith after a dream. 'To will and to run are mine, but they will cease to be mine unless God brings me His continual aid' is clear and exact.

Jerome's calling line ('should your father prostrate himself on the threshold, trample him under foot... cruelty is the only true affection') is the most vivid line in the set. But this man's family cut him off, and his mother still texts him every Eid, so it could land as pain as easily as recognition. To be fair to Jerome: he later called this letter the showy rhetoric of his youth (Letter 52, to Nepotian). Say so beside it.

Antony's lines are not his own writings. Two come from Athanasius's Life of Antony, and one is a saying passed through Evagrius and Socrates. The citation '(Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos, chapter 92, as quoted by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History)' is far too long for a phone.
Antony's calm line is a fragment that starts in lower case ('for it was neither contracted as if by grief...'), and 'it' has no antecedent.

Antony feels random as a sparring partner. His hook (walked out of church at one Gospel verse and gave everything away) is Imran's own story, and a man who fasts twice a week would admire him. The one real clash is effort, and Imran's other Disagrees are mild.
people.better: Sparring, with moderate confidence: Gregory of Nyssa, a near tie in the scorer (-0.60 against Antony's -0.62). The clashes would be on the questions Imran had to fight through with his family: whether God saves everyone (Nyssa yes; Imran a hard Disagree, thinking of his mother), whether the Bible's deeper meaning outranks the history, and how much goodness is up to us. That argument is about his life. The Antony argument is not.

problems: Cassian for a Stoic founder works, and the hook (angry at his pen, his knife and his flint) is relatable. 'Not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all' is textbook calm, and it matches his Disagree.

Cassian's lie line is cut off exactly before Cassian allows the lie. What shows is '...we must even in urgent cases of this sort speak the truth...', so it reads as if Cassian disagrees with Derek's Agree. That is a misreading of both. Use the complete sentence where Cassian compares a lie to hellebore, a dangerous medicine used only against a deadly disease (Conference 17).
Cassian's quiet line is cut off and archaic ('with lips that are dumb').

Augustine against the self-made Stoic is the classic foil, and 'Give what You command, and command what You will' is perfect against his Strongly agree on effort. But the rulers line ('a man serves God in one way in that he is man, in another way in that he is also king') shows nothing without the next sentence of Letter 185.

The Augustine line he needed is not shown. Augustine calls the Stoic ideal of feeling nothing 'worse than all vices' (City of God 14). Derek has doubted Stoic calm since sobbing at his father's funeral. That line lost the tie to 'quiet' only because of statement order and Augustine's weaker quiet cell.

A missed gift: Cassian and Augustine really did clash over grace and free will, and Cassian's Conference 13 was answered by Augustine's defender Prosper. But Cassian has no 'effort' cell in the data, so the reveal cannot say so.

The runners-up are Boethius and Clement of Alexandria, at 0.91 against 0.96. Clement wrote 'Who is the rich man that shall be saved?', which would delight a rich founder who gives quietly, and Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy. Showing them with their hooks under 'also close' would add a lot.

Origen's 'army of piety' line is the one Mennonites actually quote, and it is perfect for her Strongly disagree on war. But Origen is the most speculative mind in the pool, and she has little patience for people who talk more than they help. The other two lines do not show her.

Origen's calling line is Eusebius's narration ('he sent to his father an encouraging letter...'). It starts in lower case, has only one short sentence of Origen, and is about a son urging his father toward martyrdom. That is a strange echo of her nuanced 'the congregation should test the call first'.

Gregory the Great is a fun, fitting foil for a Mennonite: a pope praising an exarch's wars and urging a king to smash temples. But it is unfair to show only the Aethelberht letter. A few weeks later, in his letter to Mellitus (Bede, Church History 1.30), Gregory reversed it: keep the temples, destroy only the idols. Show that note or use another line.
Gregory's war line is cut off, and 'report goes that' is archaic.
The kindred margin is small: Origen 0.46, Nyssa 0.41.

The best reveal in the set. For a widower, Gregory of Nyssa's 'In no other way can the burning heart cool down... unless it relieves itself by sobs and tears' is exactly right. Nyssa also hoped all would be saved (Frank hopes for Maureen's brother), and he wrote a dialogue about death and resurrection with his dying sister.
Nyssa's anger line is long and cut off, and 'our father in God' needs explaining (it means Basil).
Nyssa's body line (On Virginity) is convoluted: 'The inefficiency of the body from either cause will be that which it guards against'. Show his 'all will be saved' cell instead.

Basil's laughter line ('there is never a time of laughter for the believer') against a man who jokes his way out of feelings is great fun. 'Whose feet then wilt thou wash?' is a gift to someone who says he hates the grief group he never misses. It has a stray space before the question mark.

Basil's 'mystery' line ('to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark') is obscure. It is about prepositions in a doxology, and nobody will see it as disagreeing with 'better left alone'.
Missed delight: the sparring partner is the kindred spirit's older brother, the one who wrote that Gregory was too simple to be trusted. The reveal should say so.

Origen fits her Strongly agrees on learning, deeper meaning and following a calling against her family. But none of the three lines touches what makes her herself: comedy, anxiety, her parents crying over law school. The calling line is Eusebius's narration about a boy urging his father to martyrdom, and it repeats his hook.
Benedict as sparring partner for a stand-up comic is ideal ('buffoonery or idle words, such as move to laughter, we utterly condemn'). She would do a bit about it.
Her Benedict lines are word for word the same three that P23 got, including the flawed learning line from Gregory's Dialogues. Friends who compare will notice the reveal is canned.

Care note: she is in recovery from an eating disorder, and Eusebius's account of Origen includes extreme fasting and self-castration. Origen's page, if she reads on, should handle his asceticism plainly and without admiration for the extremes.

Augustine for a Reformed classical homeschooler who teaches Augustine is right but expected. The calm line ('who would not consider this insensibility to be worse than all vices?') and 'not whether he is angry, but why' are excellent, and they match what she noticed about the Stoic item.
Augustine's Egyptian-gold line is cut off six words before its point ('...from those who have unlawful possession of it').

Origen's anger line is a fragment that starts with 'Besides,' and ends on a comma, and most of it is Psalm 37 ('Cease from anger, and forsake wrath'). A Bible teacher who Strongly agreed would appear to be disagreeing with a Psalm. That is awkward, and unfair to her.
Origen's 'all' line is exactly the right fight for a Westminster Confession teacher.
Missed delight: Augustine really did argue against Origen's hope that all would be restored (City of God 21). One sentence saying so would make the pair feel alive.
The kindred result is nearly a three-way tie: Augustine 0.51, Gregory the Great 0.50, Basil 0.48.

Basil is a superb match for a young man who marched against the Finance Bill and argues with his bishop father. The hook (facing down the emperor's prefect) is his story. 'Anger, stirred at the proper time and in the proper manner' fits the protester, and 'Whose feet then wilt thou wash?' fits the youth worship leader. All three lines are complete and clear.
Basil's 'Anger... is an efficient cause of manliness' is archaic, but it is fine.
Isaac is a fair, fun foil: the hermit who quit being a bishop after five months, against the activist. The laughter line is short and clear.

In Isaac, 'zeal' means a harsh zeal against other people's sins, so setting 'A zealous man will never reach peace of mind' against anger at wrongdoing is fair. But Isaac's warm hook may make Daniel like him more than argue with him. That is fine.
Isaac's citation has a stray space ('Mystic Treatises , Six Treatises...') and mixes curly and straight apostrophes.

Missed delight: Basil's faith came through his grandmother Macrina the Elder, and Daniel's through his grandmother of the East African Revival. The data cannot know this, but a hook line about Basil's grandmother would hit home.

works: Short, plain lines that answer the statement head-on are the moments that make a reveal: 'The earth belongs to all, not to the rich' (Ambrose, P22); 'To will and to run are mine, but they will cease to be mine unless God brings me His continual aid' (Jerome, P24); 'Give what You command, and command what You will' against a self-made founder (P25); the 'army of piety' for the Mennonite (P26); 'sobs and tears' for the widower (P27); Benedict condemning laughter for the comic and the sarcastic ex-evangelical (P23, P28); 'Whose feet then wilt thou wash?' (P27, P30); Augustine calling apathy 'worse than all vices' (P29).

The hooks are the strongest writing in the reveal: concrete, human and often funny (Cassian angry at his pen and flint, Benedict's bread lowered on a rope with a bell, Origen's mother hiding his clothes, Nyssa forging his uncle's letters, Basil telling the prefect that a man with only rags cannot be robbed). They create the 'I want to read more'.
Printing the player's own answer beside the early Christian's words makes the match legible and checkable. It never feels like a verdict from nowhere.

Cross-tradition surprises feel earned rather than random when the hook mirrors the person's life: the Presbyterian dawn-prayer student gets Benedict, the burned-out hiker gets Nazianzen fleeing to 'my desert, my country life, and my God', the convert who came to faith through a dream gets Jerome and his dream, and the protester gets Basil facing down the prefect.

The strongest sparring partners are classic foils that people already argue over: Augustine against the Stoic, Origen against the Westminster teacher, Gregory the Great against the Mennonite, Benedict against the comedian, Isaac against the activist.

The same line works as agreement for one person and a clash for another (Origen's 'army of piety' is P26's kindred proof and P21's and P29's sparring proof). The lines are real positions, not flattery.

Real history turns up by chance, and it is gold when it does: P25's pair (Cassian and Augustine) really fought over grace, P27's sparring partner is his kindred spirit's older brother, and P29's pair (Augustine and Origen) really disagreed about whether all will be restored.
change: Never cut a quote mid-sentence. In P21-P30, 16 of the 60 lines start in lower case, end in an ellipsis or end on a comma, and several are cut exactly before the words that carry the position. Cassian's lie line stops before he allows the lie, so it reads as the opposite. Augustine's Egyptian-gold line stops six words short. Benedict's learning line stops before 'learned ignorance'. Nazianzen's education line stops before the point. For each, pick a complete sentence of 30 words or fewer from the same passage (for Cassian, the hellebore sentence in Conference 17), or leave that cell out of line selection. Add a check to the build: every line starts with a capital and ends with . ? ! or a closing quote.

Choose the lines by what actually made the match, not by raw agreement with ties broken by statement order. score.js sorts by a*v, and the stable sort hands ties to the first statements (laugh, quiet, learning). Across all 30 people, 'learning' is shown 23 times, 'quiet' 14 and 'laugh' 15, while 'surplus' appears once and 'tears' five times. Rank lines by the centred contribution the scorer already computes. Break ties by the figure's strength (a 2 before a 1), then by a quote-quality flag (complete, own words, short). Allow each statement at most once across the six lines. That alone would have given the Stoic founder Augustine on apathy, and Kim Origen on 'God will save everyone'.

Choose the sparring partner by sharp clashes, not by the most negative average. The average can hand the result to a thinly recorded figure with small clashes (P22: Hilary at -0.37 on 6 statements, every line a -2) when another figure has three head-on -4 clashes (Chrysostom on laughter, weeping and keeping sinners out). Among the bottom third, prefer the figure with the most clashes of -3 or -4. Someone who agrees with you on half and fights you hard on three things you care about is a better 'would argue with you'.

Show only the early Christian's own words, or label clearly who is telling it. The promise is 'real words from his or her own writings', yet Benedict's learning line is Gregory the Great's narration, all three Antony lines come from Athanasius's Life or a saying passed on by Evagrius and Socrates, and Origen's calling line is Eusebius's narration ('he sent to his father...'), which also repeats his hook. Either add 'as told by Athanasius' in small type, or prefer cells in his own words.

Drop lines that need a paragraph of context to show which side the person is on: Hilary's 'It is the time to speak' (aimed at the emperor, not a view on talking less), Augustine's 'serves God as man, as king' (the point is in the next sentence), Basil's 'to investigate syllables' (about prepositions), Origen's 'Besides, the Scripture... Cease from anger' (makes the player seem to disagree with Psalm 37), Nyssa's On Virginity body sentence.

Add a fairness note wherever a line is not the person's settled view. Gregory the Great's letter to Aethelberht about overturning temples was reversed weeks later in his letter to Mellitus (keep the temples, destroy only the idols). Jerome later called his Heliodorus letter ('trample him under foot') the showy rhetoric of his youth (Letter 52). The second also matters for people estranged from family (P24).

When the two people in a result are linked in history, say so in one plain sentence. The links are all real: Basil, Gregory of Nyssa and Macrina were siblings; Basil and Nazianzen were best friends; Ambrose baptised Augustine; Cassian and Augustine's camp fought over grace; Augustine argued against Origen's restoration of all; Jerome turned on Origen and traded sharp letters with Augustine. Example: 'Your sparring partner is your kindred spirit's older brother, who wrote that he was too simple to be trusted.' That turns a good result into one people share.

Help the reader with archaic lines. Add a one-word tag to each line ('Same side' or 'Other side') so no one has to parse 'forsooth', 'wilt thou', 'dischargest' or 'Novatus' to see the point. Prefer modern translations where one exists and can be cited. Where a line is over about 25 words, add a short plain summary, clearly marked as ours.

Give the 'also close' names their hook, one line each. P25's runners-up (Boethius, and Clement, who wrote 'Who is the rich man that shall be saved?') are where a Marcus Aurelius reader's delight is. P22's kindred spirit is a coin flip (Ambrose 0.41, Nazianzen 0.40), and so is P29's (Augustine 0.51, Gregory the Great 0.50, Basil 0.48). The runner-up deserves to be seen.

Give each figure two or three quotes per strong cell, and choose by the player's answer, so friends who compare do not see word-for-word identical reveals (P23 and P28 got the same three Benedict lines).

Fill the obvious gaps in the data before the next test. Cassian has no 'effort' cell, though Conference 13 is the classic early text on grace and free will (code it from the text, as grace and will working together). Nyssa's 'all' should be preferred over his On Virginity body line wherever both qualify.

Statements. 'learning' is close to universal agreement (usual answer 1.5) and fills reveals without telling anyone anything. Sharpen it so people split (for example, about reading the best non-Christian thinkers on how to live) or keep it out of line display. 'effort' was read two ways ('a good person' as decency or as right with God, P21). 'calling' does not fit people whose family presses them toward church (P30). 'mystery' read as 'stop asking questions' to P23. Draft 2 already rewords alone, calm, pure, deeper, nature and rulers. Re-run this test on that wording.

Tidy the render: one date format for everyone ('c. 339 to 397', not a sentence), one name per work ('Rule of St Benedict' appears three ways), no stray spaces ('Letter 185 ,', 'Book 2 ,', 'wash ?'), no '--' dashes, and consistent quote marks.
